newsitem.title: USA: Developing country gold demand at record in 96 - WGC.
newsitem.headline: Developing country gold demand at record in 96 - WGC.

text.p: Demand for gold in the developing countries of Asia, the Middle East and Latin America, edged up to a record 1,825 tonnes in 1996, one percent above 1995's level, the World Gold Council (WGC) said Wednesday.
Full year 1996 demand in India moved over 500 tonnes for the first time ever, to 507.8 tonnes, a gain of six percent over 1995 levels, the WGC said.

"Demand bouyancy in the latter part of the year reflected in part the improved political and economic environment, with a stable coalition government and tighter monetary policy," WGC Americas region economist Richard Scott Ram said at a briefing on the publication of the Council's fourth quarter 1996 world gold demand survey.
Fourth quarter 1996 Indian demand was up 17 pct at 136.6 tonnes, while gold imports into India in the fourth quarter reached a record level of 76.1 tonnes.

The move by the Indian government on January 1, 1997 to allow non-resident Indians to import 10 kilograms of gold every six months, compared to five kilograms previously, is seen boosting demand this year also, Scott Ram said.
However, gold demand in China, Taiwan and Hong Kong in 1996 fell 13 pct to 371.4 tonnes.
Chinese demand fell seven percent to 207.7 tonnes in line with the generally slow retail environment, the WGC said.
With effect from January 1, 1997 though, the Peoples Bank of China announced a reduction in the domestic gold price, from $390 to $375, still above the prevailing international gold price.

Demand in Taiwan fell 23 pct to 123.3 tonnes, due to a general economic slowdown, a falling gold price which discouraged investor interest, and renewed interest in equity market investments, the WGC said.
In Hong Kong, gold demand fell six percent to 40.4 tonnes.
Gold imports into Hong Kong fell 26 pct to 193.3 tonnes in the first 11 months of 1996, as trade was diverted to other entrepot centers.
In the Middle East, demand in Dubai and Saudi Arabia was up two percent at at four year high of 237.5 tonnes in 1996.
Dubai has experienced three years of uninterrupted gold demand growth, with 1996 demand up 34 pct at 52.6 tonnes.
"Dubai is now competing with Singapore for the position of second largest physical gold distribution center in the world, behind only Switzerland," the WGC said.
Full year 1996 demand in Latin America rose an estimated 18 percent to a seven year high of 100 tonnes.
In Brazil demand rose nine percent to 59 tonnes, a seven year high, while in Mexico demand jumped 32 pct to 41 tonnes, in a rebound from the depressed 1995 performance during the peso crisis.
